Field surveys of Nemipterus bathybius in the South China Sea consistently indicate that females attain a maximum standard length of 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters], a measure that reflects the species' relatively moderate body size compared to larger congeners such as Nemipterus japonicus. This ultimate size appears to be reached after a prolonged period of somatic growth, with most individuals exceeding 18 centimeters only after their third year. At this length, the heaviest recorded individuals have an ultimate wet weight of 368 grams [Wwi = 368 grams], a mass that is typically associated with the largest, most dominant females in the population. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a predictable allometric curve, though some variation has been noted across different geographic regions, possibly linked to local prey availability and fishing pressure.

Puberty in Nemipterus bathybius is attained at a relatively small body size, with histological examination of gonadal tissue revealing that males and females first show signs of gametogenesis when they reach a standard length of 11.9 centimeters [Lp = 11.9 centimeters]. This size corresponds roughly to the midpoint of the growth trajectory for this species, suggesting that reproductive investment begins well before maximum body size is achieved. The onset of sexual maturation appears to be more closely tied to length than to age, as individuals from faster-growing cohorts tend to mature earlier. This pattern is common among tropical lutjanid and nemipterid species, where early maturation is thought to buffer against high adult mortality rates from fishing.

The early life history of Nemipterus bathybius begins with the release of pelagic eggs that measure approximately 0.8 millimeters in diameter, from which a newly hatched larva emerges with a wet weight at birth of just 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams]. This minute mass, derived from the yolk reserves of the fertilized egg, is typical of small-bodied demersal-spawning teleosts that produce numerous, small propagules as a means of maximizing larval dispersal. The yolk-sac larva remains entirely dependent on endogenous nutrients for the first several days post-hatching, a period during which rapid development of the mouthparts and digestive system occurs. The transition to first exogenous feeding is a critical bottleneck, with mortality rates exceeding ninety percent during this phase under natural conditions.

Longevity estimates for Nemipterus bathybius are based on otolith increment counts from specimens collected across its range, indicating that the maximum recorded lifespan is ten years [am = ten years] when individuals are maintained at an average water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This relatively long lifespan for a fish of its size class suggests a strategy of iteroparous reproduction, where individuals spawn repeatedly over several seasons. The thermal environment plays a key role in determining metabolic rate and thus the pace of aging, with populations inhabiting cooler waters near the lower edge of the species' thermal range showing somewhat slower growth and extended lifespans, while those in warmer equatorial waters tend to mature faster but die younger.

As part of a broader comparative analysis of life history strategies among demersal species, the maximum body mass of Nemipterus bathybius has been recorded at 368 grams [Wwi = 368 grams], a value that is notably lower than that of the sympatric Nemipterus peronii but comparable to Nemipterus zysron. The ultimate standard length of 21 cm [Li = 21 cm] is also consistent with the genus average, which typically falls between 18 and 25 centimeters for most species. These metrics, combined with a standard length at puberty of 11.9 cm [Lp = 11.9 cm], place Nemipterus bathybius firmly within the medium-bodied, early-maturing guild of the family Nemipteridae. Such life history attributes are thought to reflect an evolutionary response to the high productivity of continental shelf ecosystems, where abundant food resources support rapid juvenile growth and the onset of reproduction at a relatively small size.
